title: The evening review
hookLine: Seneca's three questions or Ignatius' gratitude
tomorrow: a monk hears one verse, says 'enough for now,' and leaves. why?

cards: Lying in bed replaying every awkward thing you said today is its own kind of trial, with no judge and no verdict. Seneca, a Roman Stoic, held a real one.

In his book On Anger he writes that when the lamp has been taken away, and his wife, who knows his habit, has gone quiet, he examines his whole day and goes back over what he did and said. He hides nothing from himself.

teach.h: WHAT HABIT HAVE I CURED TODAY?
teach.b: He learned it from the philosopher Sextius, who asked himself every night: what bad habit have I cured today? What fault have I resisted? In what way am I better?
Then Seneca reads out his own charges. In that argument, you spoke too sharply. With that man, you corrected him so bluntly that you offended him instead of helping.
And then the verdict, which is the surprise: see that you don't do that again; this time I pardon you.
That's the teaching, the Stoic evening review: an honest court, held every night, that ends in pardon rather than punishment. Seneca says the sleep that follows is sweeter.
Christians keep an evening review of their own, in their own words.
Ignatius of Loyola taught the Examen, a prayer looking back over the day that begins not with faults but with thanks for the day's gifts, and only then asks what went wrong.
Two ways of looking back, each from its own house: Seneca's three questions, or Ignatius's gratitude first. Either way, the day gets looked at once, honestly, and then put down.

how: Some readers of the Stoics review the day at night with Seneca's questions, and Christians who pray the Examen taught by Ignatius of Loyola begin it with thanks.

o: rereading old messages to see who replied to you
a written report of the day's work for your boss
looking back over the day honestly, once, before sleep

games.q: two ways to look back: tap the pairs.
p: a nightly court that ends in pardon
what bad habit have I cured today?

s: the Stoic evening review is meant to make you feel guilty
Seneca names the fault plainly, then says: this time I pardon you.
Ignatius's Examen begins with thanks before faults
it looks first for the day's gifts, then asks what went wrong.
Seneca says sleep after the review is sweeter
an honest look at the day, then rest.

games.q: your friend lies awake replaying one awkward comment from work, again and again. what would Seneca's review do differently?
o: look at it once, name what to change, pardon herself, and let it go.
keep replaying it until it stops hurting; that's what a review is.
refuse to think about the day at all and scroll until she's asleep.
games.why: Seneca's court has a verdict: the fault named once, then pardon. replaying all night is a trial that never ends.

practice: Open your notebook and write three short lines about today: one thing you're thankful for, one thing you'd do differently, and one word of pardon to yourself, the way Seneca ended his court. Keep each line plain and true.
Then close the notebook; the day has been looked at, and can be put down.

wordCard.voice: The evening review: looking back over the day honestly, once, before sleep. Seneca's nightly court; Ignatius's Examen.

orig.note: Latin: an examination, the name Ignatius's evening review is known by.

carryVoice: Your line: the review. An honest court that ends in pardon, or thanks that comes first. Two weeks of the daily practice, done.

sources.ref: Seneca, On Anger 3.36 (Sextius's nightly questions; Seneca's review after the lamp is removed; 'this time I pardon you'; sweeter sleep)
